title: Explain the prefix sum technique. How does precomputing cumulative sums let you answer range sum queries in constant time, and when should you use it?
shortTitle: Explain Prefix Sum — Precompute Cumulative Sums for O(1) Range Queries

s1_definition.profdef: A prefix sum array stores, at each index, the cumulative total of all elements up to that index. Once built in O(n) time, the sum of any contiguous range from index left to right is computed in O(1) as prefix[right plus 1] minus prefix[left], trading one-time linear preprocessing for constant-time repeated range queries.
s1_definition.analogy: The bank keeps a running total of a customer's daily deposits, so at the end of each day it writes down the cumulative balance so far. Later, to know how much was deposited between day 3 and day 7, the clerk does not re-add those days; he just subtracts the cumulative total up to day 2 from the cumulative total up to day 7. One subtraction gives the answer instantly.
s1_definition.oneliner: Precompute running totals once, then any range sum is just one subtraction of two prefix values.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A prefix sum array stores, at each index, the cumulative total of all elements up to that index. Once built in O(n) time, the sum of any contiguous range from index left to right is computed in O(1) as prefix[right plus 1] minus prefix[left], trading one-time linear preprocessing for constant-time repeated range queries.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The bank keeps a running total of a customer's daily deposits, so at the end of each day it writes down the cumulative balance so far. Later, to know how much was deposited between day 3 and day 7, the clerk does not re-add those days; he just subtracts the cumulative total up to day 2 from the cumulative total up to day 7. One subtraction gives the answer instantly.

**One line to remember:** Precompute running totals once, then any range sum is just one subtraction of two prefix values.

sections.s2_technical:
The prefix sum turns repeated range-sum work into a single subtraction. Without it, summing a range costs O(n) per query, so q queries cost O(n times q). With a prefix array, preprocessing is O(n) once and each query is O(1), so q queries cost O(n plus q).

We build the prefix array with one extra leading zero to make the math clean. For an input array of length n, the prefix array has length n plus one, where `prefix[0] = 0` and `prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + arr[i]`. The leading zero means prefix[i] is the sum of the first i elements, with no element yet at prefix[0].

A range query for the inclusive range left to right is then `prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left]`. For example, the sum of elements at indices 2 through 5 is prefix[6] minus prefix[2]. This works because prefix[6] is everything up to index 5 and prefix[2] is everything up to index 1, so the subtraction cancels the part we do not want and leaves exactly indices 2 through 5.

For money, the prefix array holds BigDecimal values and we use add and subtract, never plus and minus on primitives, to stay exact.

A senior-level nuance is that prefix sums extend to two dimensions for submatrix sums, and to prefix counts, prefix XOR, and prefix products for other range queries. The core idea, precompute a cumulative aggregate that supports an inverse operation, generalizes widely.

Another nuance is immutability. Prefix sums assume the underlying array does not change between queries; if the array is frequently updated, a Fenwick tree or segment tree is the right structure instead, because rebuilding the prefix array on every update would be O(n) per update.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India stores Rajesh's daily transaction amounts for a month, and the statement tool must answer many range queries like the total spent between any two dates. Re-summing the range on every query would be slow when the tool renders dozens of ranges for charts. This is exactly where prefix sums help.

Problem 2 — The month's data is fixed once the month closes, so it is immutable during querying, which is the precondition that makes a static prefix array the right choice rather than a Fenwick tree.

Problem 3 — Amounts are money, so the prefix array holds BigDecimal and range sums use subtract to remain exact.

In the code: a `RangeSumService` builds a BigDecimal prefix array in its constructor and answers `rangeSum(left, right)` in constant time. A `PrefixSumDemo` main builds Rajesh's daily amounts and answers several range queries.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: daily amounts 1000, 2000, 1500, 3000, 500, 2500, 4000 for days 0 to 6.

Step 1 (build): prefix[0] is 0. prefix[1] is 0 plus 1000 equals 1000. prefix[2] is 3000. prefix[3] is 4500. prefix[4] is 7500. prefix[5] is 8000. prefix[6] is 10500. prefix[7] is 14500.

Step 2 (query day 2 to 5): the answer is prefix[6] minus prefix[2], which is 10500 minus 3000 equals 7500. That equals 1500 plus 3000 plus 500 plus 2500, confirming the subtraction isolated exactly days 2 through 5.

Step 3 (query day 0 to 6): prefix[7] minus prefix[0], which is 14500 minus 0 equals 14500, the whole-week total.

Step 4 (query day 3 alone): prefix[4] minus prefix[3], which is 7500 minus 4500 equals 3000, exactly day 3's amount.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26 23:00:00 [INFO] Total spent from day 2 to day 5 (inclusive)
2026-10-26 23:00:00 [INFO] Sum -> Rs.7500
2026-10-26 23:00:00 [INFO] Total spent from day 0 to day 6 (whole week)
2026-10-26 23:00:00 [INFO] Sum -> Rs.14500
2026-10-26 23:00:00 [INFO] Total spent on day 3 alone
2026-10-26 23:00:00 [INFO] Sum -> Rs.3000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input daily: [1000 2000 1500 3000 500 2500 4000]
    │
    ▼ build prefix (leading 0), O(n)
  prefix: [0 1000 3000 4500 7500 8000 10500 14500]
    │
    ▼ query range [2..5]  →  prefix[6] - prefix[2]
                             10500 - 3000 = 7500   (O(1))
    │
    ▼ query range [0..6]  →  prefix[7] - prefix[0] = 14500
    │
    ▼ query range [3..3]  →  prefix[4] - prefix[3] = 3000
  Output: each range answered by one subtraction
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The prefix sum technique trades a one-time linear preprocessing pass for constant-time range sum queries afterwards. I build an array where each entry holds the cumulative total of all elements up to that position, and I deliberately give it a leading zero and make it one longer than the input, which makes the range math clean. After that, the sum of any contiguous range from a left index to a right index is a single subtraction, the prefix value just past the right end minus the prefix value at the left start, because that subtraction cancels everything before the range and leaves exactly the elements inside it.

The payoff is clear when there are many queries. A naive re-summing approach costs linear time per query, so many queries multiply out expensively, whereas prefix sums answer every query in constant time after the single linear build, turning an n-times-q cost into an n-plus-q cost.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this in the statement tool. Rajesh's daily transaction amounts for a closed month are fixed, and the tool renders many range totals for charts, like how much was spent between any two dates. I build a BigDecimal prefix array once and answer each range with one subtraction, which keeps the statement screen responsive even when it draws dozens of ranges.

Two points I always add show senior judgment. First, for money I keep the prefix array in BigDecimal and use add and subtract so the totals stay exact. Second, prefix sums assume the underlying data is immutable between queries, which holds for a closed month, but if the data were frequently updated I would switch to a Fenwick tree or segment tree instead, because rebuilding the prefix array on every update would cost linear time per update and defeat the purpose.
